prompts.title: Regional transit expansion
prompts.scenario: The city of Millbrook must decide how to improve commuter access. Two proposals have been put forward by the transportation committee. Using the facts below, write an essay supporting one proposal over the other. Two reasonable people could disagree based on the same information. There is no right answer.
considerations: Millbrook wants to reduce downtown traffic congestion and improve access for residents who do not own a car.
Millbrook has a limited capital budget; whichever project is chosen will absorb nearly all of it.

optionA.name: Option A: Light-rail corridor
optionA.description: Build a 12-mile light-rail line connecting the eastern suburbs to downtown. High upfront cost. Serves ~40,000 daily riders at capacity. Construction would disrupt traffic for three years. Once complete, operating costs are modest.

optionB.name: Option B: Rapid-bus network
optionB.description: Deploy a city-wide network of dedicated bus lanes with frequent service. Lower upfront cost; can be operational in 18 months. Serves more geographic area but with lower rider capacity per corridor. Operating costs are higher and ongoing.

prompts.title: Hiring a new executive director
prompts.scenario: The board of a regional food bank is selecting a new executive director. Two finalists remain. Using the facts below, write an essay supporting the hiring of one candidate over the other. There is no right answer.
considerations: The food bank wants to scale its programs into neighboring counties over the next three years.
Staff morale is low after a period of leadership turnover; retention is a concern.

optionA.name: Candidate A
optionA.description: A veteran nonprofit operator who has led two successful regional expansions. Known as demanding; several former staff cited burnout. Strong fundraising network.

optionB.name: Candidate B
optionB.description: A long-tenured internal deputy director who rose from the front lines. Beloved by staff; strong retention track record. Has never led an expansion or a capital campaign.

prompts.title: Choosing a graduate thesis topic
prompts.scenario: A graduate student must commit to a thesis topic. Two possibilities are viable. Using the facts below, write an essay supporting one topic over the other. There is no right answer.
considerations: The student wants the thesis to lead to a tenure-track faculty position.
The student wants to enjoy the work enough to sustain five years of effort.

optionA.name: Topic A: A narrow extension of the advisor's current research program
optionA.description: Well-scoped; builds on the advisor's well-funded lab. Likely to produce publishable results on schedule. The research area is crowded and trend-sensitive.

optionB.name: Topic B: An original cross-disciplinary direction the student developed independently
optionB.description: Ambitious; no established method within the advisor's lab. May open a new subfield but carries higher risk of slow progress. The student finds the question viscerally compelling.

prompts.title: Harwick City Council: Budget Reallocation for Public Infrastructure
prompts.scenario: The Harwick City Council must allocate a one-time $4.2 million capital surplus before the close of the fiscal year. The council has narrowed the choice to two projects. Each project addresses a documented municipal need, but the surplus is insufficient to fund both. The council must choose one.
considerations: The council is committed to directing capital funds toward projects with measurable near-term benefit to the largest share of residents.
The council has pledged to reduce the city's long-term maintenance liability, which has grown for three consecutive budget cycles.

optionA.name: Riverside Bridge Deck Replacement
optionA.description: The Riverside Bridge, which carries roughly 18,000 vehicle crossings per day, has a deck rated 'poor' by the state DOT and is subject to a 10-ton load restriction that reroutes commercial traffic. Full deck replacement would remove the restriction, restore full service life, and eliminate an estimated $280,000 in annual maintenance costs. The project requires a six-month lane closure affecting two bus routes.

optionB.name: Harwick Central Library HVAC Overhaul
optionB.description: The Central Library's HVAC system, installed in 1991, fails repeatedly each summer and has caused three partial closures in the past two years, displacing an average of 900 daily visitors. Replacement would restore reliable climate control, cut energy costs by an estimated $95,000 annually, and protect the library's archival collection from humidity damage. The building serves as the city's designated cooling center during heat emergencies.

prompts.title: St. Ambrose Regional Medical Center: Service Line Expansion
prompts.scenario: St. Ambrose Regional Medical Center, a 340-bed nonprofit hospital in Calloway County, has secured grant funding and capital reserves sufficient to open one new outpatient service line within the next 18 months. The hospital's board must choose between two proposals developed by its strategic planning committee.
considerations: The hospital's mission prioritizes closing documented gaps in care access for the county's underserved and uninsured populations.
The board must ensure that any new service line reaches operational self-sufficiency within three years to avoid drawing on the hospital's operating reserve.

optionA.name: Behavioral Health Urgent Care Clinic
optionA.description: Calloway County has no dedicated walk-in psychiatric or substance-use crisis service; the emergency department currently manages all acute behavioral health presentations, accounting for 22% of ED visits. The proposed clinic would provide same-day assessment, short-term stabilization, and care coordination. Reimbursement rates for behavioral health services are lower than surgical specialties, and the clinic is projected to reach break-even in month 34.

optionB.name: Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery Center
optionB.description: Residents of Calloway County currently travel an average of 47 miles for elective orthopedic procedures. The proposed ambulatory surgery center would bring sports-medicine and joint-replacement services to the county. Orthopedic procedures carry strong reimbursement margins and the center is projected to be self-sustaining by month 19. The service primarily serves insured, working-age patients rather than the county's highest-need populations.

prompts.title: Denton County Emergency Services Commission: Dispatch and Response Upgrade
prompts.scenario: The Denton County Emergency Services Commission oversees fire, EMS, and emergency dispatch for a county of 210,000 residents spread across one urban core and eleven rural townships. A federal preparedness grant provides $1.8 million, which must be obligated to a single infrastructure upgrade. The commission must choose between two options before the grant deadline.
considerations: The commission's primary mandate is to minimize preventable loss of life, measured in part by average response times across all zones.
The commission must demonstrate to county supervisors that the investment yields durable, county-wide benefit rather than concentrating resources in the urban core.

optionA.name: Next-Generation Computer-Aided Dispatch (CAD) System
optionA.description: The current CAD system is 14 years old and cannot integrate with regional mutual-aid networks or push real-time unit-location data to field crews. Replacing it would cut average dispatch-to-notify time by an estimated 90 seconds, improve resource routing across all zones, and enable automatic mutual-aid requests. Implementation requires a 10-month parallel-operation period during which dispatchers must run both systems simultaneously.

optionB.name: Three Additional Rural Quick-Response Vehicles
optionB.description: Three rural townships consistently exceed the 8-minute EMS response benchmark, with average times of 14–19 minutes due to distance from the central station. Purchasing and stationing three light-duty QRVs with ALS equipment in these townships would bring first-responder capability within 6 minutes for approximately 31,000 residents. The vehicles add ongoing maintenance and staffing costs not covered by the grant.

prompts.title: Flatlands Grain Cooperative: Equipment-Sharing Program Restructure
prompts.scenario: The Flatlands Grain Cooperative represents 84 member farms across two adjacent counties in western Kansas. A favorable equipment-financing arrangement expiring in September gives the cooperative a one-time opportunity to restructure its shared-equipment fleet. The cooperative's board must choose one of two proposals before the financing window closes.
considerations: The cooperative's bylaws require decisions to benefit the broadest practicable share of member farms, including smaller operations with fewer than 500 planted acres.
The board must keep annual fleet-operating assessments affordable enough that no member is compelled to withdraw from the cooperative.

optionA.name: Purchase Two High-Capacity Combines
optionA.description: Replacing the cooperative's aging combine fleet with two modern high-capacity units would cut per-acre harvest costs and reduce field time during the narrow Kansas harvest window. Scheduling priority would be allocated by acreage, giving larger farms earlier access and smaller farms access in the final days of optimal harvest conditions. Annual member assessments would increase by an average of $1,100.

optionB.name: Expand the Light-Equipment Pool
optionB.description: Adding four precision-planting rigs, two grain carts, and a soil-sampling unit to the shared pool would give smaller farms access to equipment they cannot individually afford, spreading productivity gains broadly. Larger member farms that already own comparable equipment would derive little additional benefit from the pool expansion. Annual assessments would increase by an average of $480.

prompts.title: Maplewood Pines Homeowners Association: Common-Area Landscape Renovation
prompts.scenario: The Maplewood Pines Homeowners Association in suburban Charlotte, North Carolina, has collected $67,000 in a dedicated landscape reserve fund over six years. The HOA board has determined that the central common area requires significant renovation and must choose between two contractor proposals before the spring planting window.
considerations: The board must maintain or increase property values within the community, as assessed landscaping quality is a documented factor in comparable home sales.
The board has committed to reducing the HOA's annual landscape maintenance contract cost, which has increased 31% over five years.

optionA.name: Traditional Ornamental Landscape Design
optionA.description: A Charlotte-based contractor proposes a formal layout of graded lawn panels, seasonal flowering beds, and a central hardscape plaza with benches and lighting. The design aligns closely with the aesthetic of comparable communities in the market area and is expected to be well-regarded by prospective buyers. Maintenance costs for the ornamental beds and turf are estimated at $18,400 annually, approximately $2,200 more than the current contract.

optionB.name: Native-Plant and Permeable-Surface Conversion
optionB.description: A landscape ecology firm proposes replacing the majority of turf with drought-tolerant native plantings, bioswales, and permeable gravel paths, eliminating irrigation system costs and reducing mowing frequency. Estimated annual maintenance drops to $9,800. The design is less conventional than neighboring communities and some residents have expressed uncertainty about its effect on curb appeal relative to traditional landscaping.

prompts.title: Cascadia Independent Film Festival: Venue Selection for Inaugural Event
prompts.scenario: The organizing committee of the Cascadia Independent Film Festival is planning its inaugural three-day event in Tacoma, Washington, scheduled for October. The committee must select a primary venue from two available options. The choice will affect programming capacity, audience experience, and the festival's ability to attract filmmakers and sponsors in its first year.
considerations: The committee wants to establish a strong public identity and generate local press coverage that will sustain the festival beyond its first year.
The festival is operating on a first-year budget of $210,000 and must not incur a deficit that would threaten a second annual event.

optionA.name: Historic Pantages Theater
optionA.description: The restored 1918 Pantages Theater seats 1,100, has an established reputation for cultural events, and is prominently featured in Tacoma tourism materials. Its rental cost is $28,000 for three days, and its single large auditorium limits simultaneous screening capacity to one program at a time. The venue's name recognition is expected to strengthen sponsorship inquiries and press interest.

optionB.name: Tacoma Art Museum Flex Galleries
optionB.description: The TAM's reconfigurable gallery spaces can support three simultaneous screenings for audiences of 80–150, enabling a richer program schedule and more filmmaker Q&A sessions. The rental cost is $11,500 for three days, preserving budget for filmmaker travel stipends. The space lacks theatrical atmosphere and has no prior identity as a film venue, which may make it harder to convey the festival's ambitions to first-year sponsors.

prompts.title: Lodestar Analytics: Go-to-Market Strategy for First Commercial Product
prompts.scenario: Lodestar Analytics, a twelve-person B2B software startup based in Austin, Texas, has completed development of a supply-chain forecasting tool and must launch its commercial go-to-market effort within 90 days. The company has $900,000 in runway and no existing paying customers. The founding team must choose between two launch strategies.
considerations: Lodestar must generate sufficient revenue within 14 months to qualify for its Series A financing round, for which lead investors have set a minimum annual-recurring-revenue threshold.
The founding team believes that reference customers with recognizable names will be critical to closing enterprise deals in year two.

optionA.name: Direct Enterprise Sales Motion
optionA.description: Lodestar would hire two senior enterprise account executives immediately and pursue a short list of 15 Fortune 500 logistics and retail targets identified during beta development. Average contract value is projected at $180,000 ARR, meaning three closed deals would satisfy the Series A threshold. Enterprise sales cycles typically run 9–14 months, and there is meaningful execution risk that no deal closes before runway is exhausted.

optionB.name: Product-Led Growth via Mid-Market Self-Service
optionB.description: Lodestar would offer a freemium tier targeting mid-market distributors, supported by a lightweight inside-sales team. Average contract value is projected at $22,000 ARR, requiring roughly 25 conversions to meet the Series A threshold. Conversion cycles are shorter—typically 30–60 days—and the model generates customer volume more quickly. However, mid-market logos are less prestigious and may carry less weight with the Series A lead investors.

prompts.title: Whitmore University Center for Structural Biology: Major Equipment Acquisition
prompts.scenario: The Whitmore University Center for Structural Biology has received a $1.4 million equipment allocation from the university's research capital fund. The center director must select one instrument for purchase before the fiscal year ends. The choice will shape the center's research capabilities for at least a decade.
considerations: The center director is under pressure from the dean to attract externally funded grants, particularly those from NIH and NSF programs, within the next three years.
The center must serve graduate training needs across three departments, and the instrument should be accessible to researchers at varying levels of technical expertise.

optionA.name: Cryo-Electron Microscope (Cryo-EM)
optionA.description: A cryo-EM would position Whitmore at the frontier of macromolecular structure determination, a field currently drawing large NIH program-project grants. The instrument costs $1.35 million, leaving a thin margin for installation and maintenance. Operation requires a dedicated specialist, and its complexity limits use by early-stage graduate students without substantial training investment. Comparable cryo-EM facilities at three regional institutions create potential collaborative redundancy.

optionB.name: High-Field Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectrometer
optionB.description: A 600 MHz NMR spectrometer costs $980,000, leaving over $400,000 for maintenance contracts, consumables, and a part-time instrument manager. NMR supports a wider range of projects across chemistry, biochemistry, and pharmacology and is routinely used by first-year graduate students. The technique is more established and attracts a broad but less concentrated pool of smaller individual investigator grants rather than large program awards.

prompts.title: City of Portsmith Parking Authority: Downtown Parking Strategy
prompts.scenario: The Portsmith Parking Authority must decide how to address a documented shortfall of approximately 600 daytime parking spaces in the city's core commercial district by 2027. Two proposals have cleared environmental and zoning review, but funding is available for only one. The authority's board must make a final selection.
considerations: The authority is required by city charter to support the economic vitality of downtown merchants, several of whom have cited parking as a factor in declining foot traffic.
The authority must avoid increasing its long-term debt burden beyond the level approved in the current five-year capital plan.

optionA.name: New Six-Story Parking Structure on Elm Lot
optionA.description: Constructing a 720-space garage on the city-owned Elm Street surface lot would fully resolve the projected shortfall and add a net 580 spaces. Total project cost is $21 million, requiring $14 million in revenue bonds above the current capital plan ceiling. The structure would take 28 months to build, during which the existing 140-space surface lot would be unavailable. Structured parking is expected to generate sufficient fee revenue to service the debt over 20 years.

optionB.name: Dynamic Pricing and Shared-Use Agreement Program
optionB.description: Installing a real-time pricing and wayfinding system across all existing city lots, combined with negotiated evening-and-weekend shared-use agreements with four private garage operators, would make an estimated 410 additional spaces effectively available during peak demand. Total program cost is $2.9 million, well within the current capital plan. The approach does not add permanent capacity and relies on continued private-operator cooperation, which is not guaranteed beyond initial five-year agreements.

prompts.title: Harvest Bridge Food Bank: Regional Distribution Network Restructure
prompts.scenario: Harvest Bridge Food Bank, which serves a nine-county region in rural western Virginia, must restructure its distribution network after losing the lease on its central warehouse. The organization has 18 months before the facility closure and must select one of two operational models. The decision will define how the organization functions for the foreseeable future.
considerations: Harvest Bridge's board has committed to maintaining or improving the frequency and volume of food delivery to the approximately 14,000 households it currently serves, with particular attention to households in the most remote townships.
The organization depends heavily on volunteer labor and must not adopt a model that requires staffing levels it cannot sustain with its current $2.1 million annual operating budget.

optionA.name: Hub-and-Spoke Model with New Leased Central Facility
optionA.description: Harvest Bridge would lease a replacement central warehouse in Albemarle County and operate a scheduled weekly delivery route to 22 partner pantries across the nine counties. The centralized model allows bulk purchasing, cold-chain management, and consistent quality control. Annual facility and transport costs are projected at $490,000, a $140,000 increase over current expenses, and the model requires three additional part-time logistics staff.

optionB.name: Decentralized Partner-Pantry Autonomy Model
optionB.description: Rather than replacing the central warehouse, Harvest Bridge would redistribute procurement authority to its 22 partner pantries, each of which would manage its own regional food sourcing with coordination support and a shared purchasing account. Overhead costs drop significantly and no new lease is required, keeping expenses within the current budget. Pantry capacity and volunteer reliability vary widely across the network, and the model reduces Harvest Bridge's ability to ensure equitable distribution to the most isolated communities.

prompts.title: Hargrove Regional Medical Center: Expanding Specialty Services
prompts.scenario: Hargrove Regional Medical Center, a mid-sized hospital in Decatur, Illinois, must decide how to expand its clinical capacity. The hospital's board of directors has approved funding for one expansion initiative. The board must choose between two options.
considerations: Hargrove Regional seeks to reduce patient out-migration—the rate at which insured local residents travel to larger metro hospitals for procedures unavailable at Hargrove.
The expansion must be financially self-sustaining within four years; the hospital carries existing debt from a 2019 facility renovation and cannot absorb prolonged operating losses.
Hargrove serves a catchment area with a high proportion of elderly Medicare patients and a growing population of working-age adults with employer-sponsored insurance.

Community trust is a strategic priority: hospital leadership has publicly committed to expanding services that address documented gaps in local care rather than duplicating services already available from a competing clinic nearby.

optionA.name: Cardiac Catheterization Lab
optionA.description: Hargrove would build and staff a cardiac catheterization laboratory, enabling interventional cardiology procedures currently unavailable within 60 miles. The lab requires a $4.2 million capital outlay and recruitment of two interventional cardiologists, but reimbursement rates for cardiac procedures are among the highest in inpatient medicine, and local cardiologists have documented referral demand. The lab would not reach break-even until year three under conservative volume projections.

optionB.name: Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery Center
optionB.description: Hargrove would open a dedicated outpatient orthopedic surgery center offering joint-replacement and sports-medicine procedures on an ambulatory basis. Startup costs are lower at $2.6 million, and the center could reach profitability within 18 months given established volume from the hospital's existing orthopedic group. However, a competing orthopedic practice two miles away already offers overlapping elective procedures, which may limit incremental patient capture and draw community scrutiny.

prompts.title: Maplewood Unified School District: Restructuring the Academic Calendar
prompts.scenario: The Maplewood Unified School District in central Oregon serves approximately 11,400 students across fourteen schools. The superintendent and school board must adopt a new academic calendar beginning with the 2026–2027 school year. The board must choose between two options.
considerations: Maplewood's standardized test scores in reading and mathematics have declined for three consecutive years, and district leadership has identified summer learning loss as a contributing factor.

Families and staff have raised strong concerns about predictability; any calendar change must provide at least one continuous break of no fewer than four weeks to accommodate family vacations and teacher professional-development programs.

The district operates under a collective-bargaining agreement requiring that any change in instructional days be negotiated with the teachers' union; union leadership has signaled openness to modification but has conditioned support on preserved total compensation.

Several Maplewood schools double as community emergency-shelter sites, and the county emergency-management office has requested that at least one school facility remain available for activation during peak wildfire season in July and August.

optionA.name: Balanced (Year-Round) Calendar
optionA.description: The district would shift to a 45-15 balanced calendar, with students attending school in nine-week blocks separated by three-week intersessions throughout the year. This structure virtually eliminates the traditional summer gap and allows the district to offer voluntary intersession remediation programs. However, the calendar compresses all school breaks into shorter windows, complicating family scheduling, and requires renegotiated custodial and food-service contracts that district analysts estimate will increase operating costs by roughly $870,000 annually.

optionB.name: Extended Traditional Calendar
optionB.description: The district would retain a modified traditional calendar, starting three weeks earlier in mid-July and ending in early June, adding eight instructional days while preserving a six-week summer break. The extended calendar requires minimal contractual renegotiation and keeps costs nearly flat. Critics note, however, that beginning school in mid-July conflicts with peak wildfire season, potentially forcing school closures that offset any instructional gains, and the shortened summer does not address the multi-month learning-loss pattern research has associated with traditional schedules.

prompts.title: Vanthorpe Institute for Atmospheric Research: Major Equipment Acquisition
prompts.scenario: The Vanthorpe Institute for Atmospheric Research, a federally funded laboratory in Boulder, Colorado, has received a one-time capital equipment allocation of $1.8 million from its parent agency. The institute's director and equipment committee must select a single acquisition. The committee must choose between two options.
considerations: Vanthorpe's five-year strategic plan prioritizes publishing high-impact research in peer-reviewed journals, with particular emphasis on data that can directly inform federal climate modeling initiatives.

The institute's grant pipeline depends on maintaining technical capabilities competitive with peer laboratories; the committee is aware that two rival institutions recently upgraded their remote-sensing arrays.

Vanthorpe employs six early-career researchers whose continued employment is contingent on obtaining external grants; equipment that broadens grant-application eligibility is therefore of institutional importance.
The institute's equipment maintenance budget is fixed at $140,000 per year and cannot be increased without a separate appropriations request to the agency.

optionA.name: Doppler Wind Lidar System
optionA.description: Vanthorpe would purchase a state-of-the-art ground-based Doppler wind lidar capable of profiling atmospheric boundary-layer dynamics at unprecedented vertical resolution. The system costs $1.75 million and has annual maintenance costs of $95,000, comfortably within budget. It directly supports two active federally funded projects and would give the institute a capability no peer lab currently possesses in the region. However, the lidar's highly specialized application limits its utility to a narrow subset of ongoing research programs and may not broaden grant eligibility for early-career staff working outside boundary-layer science.

optionB.name: High-Resolution Mass Spectrometry Cluster
optionB.description: Vanthorpe would acquire a cluster of three high-resolution aerosol mass spectrometers, enabling simultaneous multi-site atmospheric chemistry measurements. The cluster costs $1.62 million, leaving a modest capital reserve, but carries combined annual maintenance of $135,000—near the ceiling of the fixed maintenance budget. The spectrometers are applicable across a wider range of research programs, potentially strengthening grant applications for several early-career researchers, but the capability partially overlaps with instrumentation already available at a nearby university laboratory with which Vanthorpe has a data-sharing agreement.

prompts.title: Sycamore Pines Retirement Community: New Amenity Development
prompts.scenario: Sycamore Pines, a continuing-care retirement community in Scottsdale, Arizona, has secured $900,000 from its capital reserve fund for a single new resident amenity. The community's amenity committee—composed of the executive director, two board members, and three elected resident representatives—must select one project. The committee must choose between two options.
considerations: Sycamore Pines competes for prospective residents with four other upscale retirement communities in the Phoenix metropolitan area; marketing leadership has identified amenity differentiation as a primary driver of move-in decisions among prospects touring the community.

The community's resident population skews older than its peer facilities, with a median age of 81; a significant portion of residents have mobility limitations that constrain participation in strenuous physical activities.

Sycamore Pines operates under Arizona's continuing-care regulations, which require maintenance of a 120-day operating cash reserve; any amenity that generates ongoing staffing costs must be shown to be revenue-neutral or better within two years.
Resident council surveys conducted in 2024 showed near-equal interest in wellness programming and in social and creative-arts activities, with no single preference commanding a clear majority.

optionA.name: Aquatic Therapy and Warm-Water Pool
optionA.description: Sycamore Pines would construct a therapeutic warm-water pool with ADA-compliant entry features and contract with a licensed aquatic therapist to lead daily group sessions and individual rehabilitation appointments, the latter billable to Medicare Part B. The pool addresses mobility-related needs broadly and could generate partial revenue through therapy billing, though construction bids have come in at $880,000, leaving little capital contingency. Operating costs, net of projected therapy revenue, are estimated at $60,000 annually—a figure that may challenge the two-year revenue-neutrality requirement if therapy utilization falls short of projections.

optionB.name: Creative Arts and Technology Center
optionB.description: Sycamore Pines would convert an underused multipurpose room into a dedicated creative arts and technology center equipped with pottery kilns, digital design workstations, a recording studio alcove, and high-speed fabrication tools. The build-out and equipment cost $740,000, leaving a meaningful capital reserve. The center requires only a part-time coordinator ($38,000 annually) and is expected to be easily revenue-neutral. However, the center's physical activities are less accessible to residents with significant mobility limitations, and peer communities have not yet offered comparable technology-arts programming, making market differentiation harder to quantify.

prompts.title: Cascade Rim National Park: Visitor Infrastructure Expansion
prompts.scenario: Cascade Rim National Park, located in southern Washington State, has been allocated $6 million in federal infrastructure funds under a multi-year improvement program. The park superintendent must submit a project selection to the regional National Park Service director. The superintendent must choose between two options.
considerations: Cascade Rim recorded 1.4 million visitors in 2024, a 38 percent increase over 2019; resource managers have identified visitor-concentration damage to sensitive riparian and alpine ecosystems along the park's most trafficked corridors.
The park's enabling legislation requires that infrastructure investments preserve or enhance the visitor experience while demonstrating minimal long-term impact on natural resources.

Adjacent gateway communities—particularly the town of Ridgefall, population 4,200—depend economically on park tourism and have lobbied the NPS for improvements that extend visitor dwell time and overnight stays.
The park currently has no reliable broadband or cellular connectivity in its interior, which has complicated emergency response coordination in three incidents over the past two years.

optionA.name: Northern Trailhead Dispersal Hub
optionA.description: The park would construct a new trailhead complex on the less-visited northern boundary, including a 200-vehicle parking facility, a visitor orientation center, two miles of new hardened trail connecting to the existing trail network, and a shuttle staging area. The project is projected to redirect up to 30 percent of current peak-day visitors away from the degraded southern corridor. It does not address emergency-communications gaps and may draw some visitation away from Ridgefall, which is located near the southern entrance.

optionB.name: Southern Corridor Hardening and Digital Infrastructure
optionB.description: The park would invest in armoring and boardwalking 4.5 miles of the most ecologically damaged southern trail segments, constructing composting restroom facilities at three high-use nodes, and installing a low-impact distributed antenna system providing emergency-grade communications throughout the park interior. The project protects the most threatened ecosystems and resolves the communications gap but does not reduce visitor concentration—it accommodates existing traffic rather than redistributing it—and provides no new visitor amenity likely to increase overnight stays benefiting Ridgefall.

prompts.title: Delvara Consumer Products: Timing a New Product Launch
prompts.scenario: Delvara Consumer Products, a mid-market household goods company headquartered in Minneapolis, has completed development of a next-generation air-purification device, the AirMesh 3. The company's executive team must decide when and how to bring the product to market. The team must choose between two options.
considerations: Delvara's market research indicates a primary competitor, HaloAir, is developing a comparable device and is expected to announce within six to nine months; the executive team believes first-mover status in the premium air-purification segment carries a significant and durable pricing advantage.

The AirMesh 3 relies on a proprietary filter cartridge; Delvara's supply-chain team has confirmed it can produce 80,000 units in the first production run but cannot guarantee quality-control consistency beyond that volume for at least twelve months.

Delvara's retail partners—principally three national big-box chains—have requested exclusivity windows and have conditioned preferred shelf placement on receiving adequate initial inventory to avoid stock-outs during the first 60 days.

Consumer reviews are the dominant purchase-driver in the air-purification category; a product launch accompanied by quality defects or stock-outs has historically caused lasting reputational damage disproportionate to the incident's scope.

optionA.name: Immediate Broad Retail Launch
optionA.description: Delvara would launch the AirMesh 3 nationwide across all three retail partners simultaneously within six weeks, committing the full 80,000-unit first run to shelf inventory. This approach maximizes first-mover advantage and fulfills retailer exclusivity terms, securing premium shelf placement before any HaloAir announcement. However, the full allocation leaves no inventory buffer for online direct-to-consumer sales, and distributing the run across three large chains risks localized stock-outs if regional demand proves uneven—conditions that prior category launches suggest are likely in the first 90 days.

optionB.name: Phased Regional and Direct-to-Consumer Launch
optionB.description: Delvara would launch first through its own e-commerce platform and through one retail partner in three pilot markets, using approximately 35,000 units, then expand nationally after the supply chain scales in roughly twelve months. The phased approach allows quality monitoring and demand calibration before full retail commitment, reducing the risk of a defect-driven reputational incident. However, the delayed national presence may allow HaloAir to announce or launch during the interim, eroding the first-mover premium and potentially forcing Delvara into less favorable retail terms the following year.

prompts.title: Riverside Community Food Bank: Distribution Network Restructuring
prompts.scenario: Riverside Community Food Bank in Fresno, California, distributes approximately 2.4 million pounds of food annually through a network of partner agencies and direct-distribution events. The food bank's executive director and operations committee must restructure the distribution model in response to a 22 percent increase in client demand recorded over the past 18 months. The committee must choose between two options.
considerations: Riverside's funding comes predominantly from individual donors and two anchor foundation grants; both foundations have indicated continued support contingent on the food bank demonstrating expanded geographic reach into rural communities in the eastern part of Fresno County that are currently underserved.

The food bank's volunteer base—approximately 340 active volunteers—is concentrated in the city of Fresno and has limited availability to support operations at remote sites more than 20 miles from the central warehouse.

Perishable food—produce, dairy, and protein—represents 58 percent of Riverside's inventory by weight and requires refrigerated transport and short distribution windows; the food bank currently operates two refrigerated trucks.

Riverside's operations team has identified significant duplication of effort with three smaller partner food pantries in central Fresno whose client populations substantially overlap with Riverside's direct-distribution sites.

optionA.name: Mobile Rural Distribution Expansion
optionA.description: Riverside would lease a third refrigerated truck and establish bi-weekly mobile distribution stops at six rural eastern-county locations, prioritizing the underserved communities flagged by foundation funders. The food bank would partner with local churches and community centers to provide minimal on-site volunteer support, reducing but not eliminating the distance burden on the central volunteer corps. The model does not address the duplication with central-Fresno partner pantries and will strain the operations team, which currently runs near capacity.

optionB.name: Agency Consolidation and Hub-and-Spoke Redesign
optionB.description: Riverside would formalize a hub-and-spoke model by absorbing two of the three overlapping central-Fresno partner pantries into a coordinated distribution schedule, eliminating redundancy and freeing roughly $180,000 in annual operational cost. Savings would fund capacity upgrades at the central warehouse and a contracted rural-delivery partnership with a regional logistics provider for eastern-county drops twice monthly. The consolidation will require complex negotiations with partner agencies and may temporarily reduce service frequency in central Fresno during a 4–6 month transition, affecting existing clients.

prompts.title: Ironwood Community Foundation: Annual Fundraising Event Format
prompts.scenario: The Ironwood Community Foundation in Providence, Rhode Island, raises approximately $1.1 million annually to fund local arts, education, and social-service grants. Its board of directors must decide on the format for the 2026 signature fundraising event, which has historically accounted for $340,000—nearly one-third of annual revenue. The board must choose between two options.
considerations: Ironwood's donor base is bifurcated: approximately 60 major donors contributing gifts of $5,000 or more account for 70 percent of event revenue, while a broader base of 400–500 mid-level donors contributes the remainder; the board has identified major-donor stewardship as its highest retention priority.

The foundation's strategic plan calls for expanding its donor base by engaging younger professional philanthropists (ages 30–45) in Providence, a segment that has shown low participation in the foundation's traditional black-tie gala format.

Ironwood's 2025 event generated criticism from several longtime major donors who felt the program was too long and insufficiently focused on showcasing grant impact; two of those donors subsequently reduced their pledges.

The foundation operates with a three-person development staff and relies heavily on a volunteer event committee of twelve; any event format that substantially increases logistical complexity risks exhausting staff capacity during the foundation's concurrent spring grant cycle.

optionA.name: Reimagined Signature Gala
optionA.description: Ironwood would retain the black-tie gala format but restructure the program significantly: shortening the formal program to 45 minutes, replacing a lengthy awards segment with a curated video showcase of grant impact, and adding a post-dinner reception with grantee representatives for direct donor interaction. The redesigned gala is projected to recover the dissatisfied major donors and maintain premium ticket pricing. However, the format remains unlikely to attract the younger professional demographic Ironwood seeks, and production costs for a high-quality video package and redesigned venue experience are estimated at $28,000 more than the 2025 event.

optionB.name: Multi-Site Neighborhood Celebration Series
optionB.description: Ironwood would replace the single gala with a series of three smaller evening events hosted in distinct Providence neighborhoods, each featuring a local chef, live music by a grant-funded arts organization, and intimate roundtable conversations with foundation leaders. Ticket prices would be set lower to attract mid-level and younger donors, and each event would have a neighborhood-specific grant-impact theme. Revenue projections are less certain and could fall short of the gala benchmark if major donors choose not to attend multiple events; the three-event format also significantly increases logistical demands on the development staff and volunteer committee.

prompts.title: Halcyon Court Apartments: Major Building Renovation Prioritization
prompts.scenario: Halcyon Court, a 220-unit apartment complex in Durham, North Carolina, is owned by a regional property management firm, Piedmont Residential LLC. The firm has secured financing for one major renovation project to be completed before lease renewals are renegotiated in 18 months. Leadership must choose between two options.
considerations: Halcyon Court's current occupancy rate is 91 percent, below the firm's 95 percent target; exit surveys from non-renewing tenants over the past two years cite dated unit interiors and unreliable HVAC systems as the top two reasons for departure.

Piedmont Residential is pursuing a portfolio refinancing in approximately 24 months; lenders have indicated that demonstrated rent-growth trajectory and occupancy improvement are the primary underwriting factors for favorable terms.

The Durham rental market has tightened, with average market rents for comparable properties increasing 11 percent over the past 18 months; Piedmont has not raised rents at Halcyon Court commensurately, in part because management has been reluctant to increase rents without corresponding amenity or unit improvements.

Halcyon Court's HVAC infrastructure is 19 years old; the property's mechanical contractor has advised that at least 40 units are at elevated risk of system failure in the next 12–24 months, which would trigger emergency repair costs and potential habitability complaints.

optionA.name: Full Unit Interior Renovation Program
optionA.description: Piedmont would renovate all 220 units with new cabinetry, countertops, flooring, and fixtures on a rolling basis as units turn over, plus upgrade the leasing office and fitness center. The program costs $2.9 million and is designed to justify rent increases averaging $175 per month on renovated units, supporting both occupancy recovery and the rent-growth narrative needed for refinancing. The program does not address the aging HVAC infrastructure; emergency mechanical failures during the renovation period would require unplanned expenditures and could disrupt construction scheduling.

optionB.name: HVAC System Replacement and Common-Area Modernization
optionB.description: Piedmont would replace HVAC systems in all 220 units and undertake targeted common-area upgrades—resurfacing the pool deck, replacing corridor lighting with LED systems, and adding package-locker infrastructure—at a total cost of $2.6 million. The mechanical replacement eliminates the failure risk and reduces resident maintenance complaints, a factor that management believes contributes to turnover, and improves energy efficiency. However, HVAC replacement is less visible to prospective tenants than interior renovations, may support only modest rent increases ($60–$80 per month on average), and produces a weaker rent-growth narrative for the upcoming refinancing.

prompts.title: Aldgate Community Theater: Selecting the 2026–2027 Season
prompts.scenario: Aldgate Community Theater in Ann Arbor, Michigan, is a nonprofit producing organization with an annual operating budget of $520,000. Its artistic director and board programming committee must finalize the 2026–2027 main-stage season, which will consist of four productions and anchor the organization's subscription campaign launching in February 2026. The committee must choose between two season configurations.
considerations: Aldgate's subscriber base of 1,140 households skews toward patrons over 55 who have historically responded most strongly to familiar titles and classic American and British drama; subscriber retention is the theater's primary earned-revenue driver.

The theater received a $75,000 capacity-building grant from a regional arts foundation conditioned on demonstrated commitment to producing work by living playwrights from underrepresented communities, with a progress report due in October 2026.

Aldgate's production budget is tightest for shows requiring large casts, elaborate sets, or licensed orchestrations; the theater has struggled to break even on musicals in two of the last three seasons due to royalty and musician costs.

Ann Arbor's competitive performing-arts landscape includes the University of Michigan's professional series and two other community companies; the artistic director believes Aldgate must develop a distinctive programming identity to avoid direct competition.

optionA.name: Classic-Anchor Season with One New Work
optionA.description: The season would open with Arthur Miller's All My Sons, follow with a production of Noël Coward's Private Lives, include a small-cast contemporary comedy by a mid-career playwright, and close with a well-known American musical. This configuration is designed to maximize subscription appeal to the existing over-55 base and minimize risk in the renewal campaign. The single contemporary work partially addresses the grant conditions, but foundation program officers have informally indicated they expect more substantive commitment to new work, and the closing musical carries royalty and orchestra costs that have historically compressed margins.

optionB.name: New-Work-Forward Season with One Classic Anchor
optionB.description: The season would open with a world-premiere play by a Detroit-based playwright of Dominican heritage, follow with a regional-premiere work by a Native American dramatist, include a mid-century classic (Lorraine Hansberry's A Raisin in the Sun) as the season's anchor, and close with a small-cast contemporary drama. The configuration robustly fulfills the grant conditions and positions Aldgate distinctly in the local landscape. However, the absence of immediately recognizable titles in three of four slots may complicate the subscription campaign, and subscriber research suggests that two or more unfamiliar titles in a season has historically correlated with a 12–18 percent renewal decline among the over-55 cohort.

prompts.title: Hartwell Public Library: Staffing Model Transition
prompts.scenario: The Hartwell Public Library board must decide how to address a staffing crisis after three veteran reference librarians announced retirement in the same fiscal year. The library serves a mid-sized city of 84,000 residents, operates on a fixed municipal budget, and has a stated mission of maximizing equitable access to research assistance and community programming. The board is choosing between two staffing models to be implemented at the start of the next fiscal year.
considerations: The library must maintain or improve the quality of research assistance available to patrons, including underserved populations with limited digital literacy.
The library's operating budget cannot be increased; any staffing solution must be cost-neutral or cost-reducing over a three-year horizon.
The library has a secondary mission to expand community programming, including children's literacy events and job-search workshops.
Staff morale and institutional continuity matter; the remaining six full-time employees have expressed concern about workload and direction.

optionA.name: Hire Two Specialized Librarians
optionA.description: The library fills two of the three vacancies with credentialed reference librarians, one specializing in digital services and one in youth programming. The third position is eliminated, producing a modest budget savings redirected toward extended evening hours. This maintains professional expertise in high-demand service areas but leaves the overall headcount reduced, increasing workload for remaining staff.

optionB.name: Adopt a Paraprofessional Staffing Model
optionB.description: All three vacancies are filled with paraprofessional library associates at a lower salary tier, overseen by a newly designated lead librarian promoted from existing staff. The cost savings fund a part-time community outreach coordinator. This expands the library's programming capacity and keeps headcount stable but replaces credentialed expertise with staff who have narrower formal training in research assistance.

prompts.title: Coastline Independent Film Festival: Venue Selection
prompts.scenario: The board of the Coastline Independent Film Festival, held annually in Pelican Cove, must choose a primary screening venue for its upcoming three-year contract cycle. Attendance has grown 40 percent over five years, straining the festival's current informal arrangement with a local high school auditorium. The board must sign a venue contract before the end of the month. Two options have cleared initial negotiations.
considerations: The festival must accommodate reliable growth in ticketed attendance while keeping per-ticket costs low enough to preserve its accessible, community-oriented identity.
Technical screening quality — including digital projection, sound isolation, and disabled-access seating — is central to the festival's reputation among filmmakers and press.
The venue contract will span three years; flexibility for scheduling across a ten-day festival window is essential.
The festival depends on local sponsorship; the chosen venue's visibility and civic associations affect sponsor interest.

optionA.name: Harborview Performing Arts Center
optionA.description: A renovated municipal arts center with a 620-seat main hall, full 4K projection, and dedicated green-room facilities. Its central downtown location offers high foot traffic and sponsor visibility, and the facility management will accommodate all ten festival days. However, the rental rate is 55 percent higher than the festival's current arrangement, requiring either a ticket price increase or a new sponsorship commitment to remain budget-neutral.

optionB.name: Calloway University Cinema Complex
optionB.description: A university-owned, three-screen cinema built in 2019 with state-of-the-art projection and sound in each auditorium, offering combined seating of 780 across screens. The university will discount the rental in exchange for co-branding and two reserved campus-community screening nights, keeping costs within budget. The campus location sits two miles from downtown, which may reduce walk-in attendance and complicate logistics for evening events.

prompts.title: City of Drescott: Downtown Parking Strategy
prompts.scenario: The Drescott City Council must adopt a long-term downtown parking policy to address chronic weekday congestion, declining retail foot traffic, and the impending expiration of a lease on its largest surface lot. The policy will govern parking infrastructure investment and pricing for at least a decade. The council has narrowed the choice to two strategies after eighteen months of public input and traffic studies.
considerations: The council seeks to reduce vehicle congestion on core downtown streets without displacing shoppers or workers who depend on affordable parking.
Downtown retail vacancy is at 18 percent; the council views accessible parking as one lever for reversing merchant attrition.
The city has committed to reducing per-capita vehicle emissions by 15 percent within ten years as part of a regional climate agreement.
Capital outlays must be financed within the city's existing bonding capacity; operating costs must be self-sustaining within five years.

optionA.name: Build a Central Parking Structure
optionA.description: The city constructs a 900-space, municipally owned parking garage on the expiring surface-lot parcel, funded through a 20-year revenue bond. Monthly permit rates and hourly fees are projected to service the debt within six years. The garage consolidates parking demand, frees curb lanes for bike infrastructure, and signals investment in downtown vitality. However, it locks in car-dependent infrastructure for decades and does little to reduce total vehicle trips to the core.

optionB.name: Implement Dynamic Pricing and Transit Incentives
optionB.description: The city converts all remaining surface lots and on-street spaces to demand-responsive pricing managed by a third-party platform, using variable rates to keep occupancy near 85 percent. Revenue above operating costs subsidizes expanded bus-rapid-transit service on two downtown corridors and a merchant-validated parking voucher program. This approach requires no new construction debt but depends on behavioral change and carries uncertainty about whether transit improvements will be built out on schedule.

prompts.title: Merrow County Solid Waste Authority: Waste-Management Approach
prompts.scenario: The Merrow County Solid Waste Authority board must select a new primary waste-management approach before its contract with a regional landfill expires in fourteen months. The county generates approximately 210,000 tons of municipal solid waste annually, and the landfill contract renewal would carry a 30 percent rate increase. Two alternative approaches have completed feasibility review. The board's decision will govern county waste operations for a minimum of fifteen years.
considerations: The authority is legally obligated to manage all residential and commercial waste without interruption; any transition risk must be kept within acceptable operational bounds.
Long-term cost predictability is essential; the authority's funding comes from fixed residential tipping fees that are politically difficult to raise.
The county has adopted a Zero Waste resolution targeting 60 percent landfill diversion by 2035.
The authority employs 140 workers whose job security and working conditions are subject to a collective bargaining agreement expiring in two years.

optionA.name: Construct a County-Owned Composting and Materials Recovery Facility
optionA.description: The authority bonds $48 million to build a combined composting and single-stream recycling facility on county-owned land, projected to divert 55 percent of the waste stream and reduce landfill dependency to a small residual fraction. The facility would retain all current employees under an expanded job classification agreement. Tipping fees are projected to stabilize after a ten-year debt-service period, but construction delays or processing shortfalls could leave the authority exposed during the transition.

optionB.name: Enter a Long-Term Waste-to-Energy Contract
optionB.description: The authority signs a 20-year processing agreement with Renovo Energy Partners, which will accept all residual waste at a fixed escalating rate capped at CPI plus one percent. The agreement includes a county recycling drop-off expansion funded by Renovo. This eliminates capital risk and guarantees processing continuity but diversion rates under the model are projected to reach only 38 percent by 2035, falling short of the Zero Waste resolution target. It also reduces direct county control over operations and may affect labor classifications under the existing collective bargaining agreement.

prompts.title: Ardent Consumer Goods: New Product Launch Decision
prompts.scenario: The executive team at Ardent Consumer Goods, a regional household-products company with $220 million in annual revenue, must decide how to launch its first entry into the premium cleaning-products category. Eighteen months of R&D have produced a plant-based, concentrated cleaning line called Verdant. The product has cleared regulatory review, and the team must commit to a launch strategy before a major trade show in eleven weeks. Two approaches have been developed by the marketing and sales divisions.
considerations: Ardent's core strength is its existing relationships with 1,200 independent grocery and hardware retailers in the mid-Atlantic region; channel strategy should protect those relationships.
The premium cleaning category is crowded with national brands; Verdant's differentiation depends on conveying concentrated-formula value and environmental credentials to a skeptical consumer.
The company's working capital position limits upfront marketing investment to approximately $3.2 million for the first twelve months.
Internal growth targets require Verdant to reach $8 million in net sales within 18 months of launch.

optionA.name: Regional Retail Launch with In-Store Activation
optionA.description: Ardent launches Verdant exclusively through its existing independent retailer network, supported by in-store end-cap displays, a shelf-talker campaign emphasizing the concentration value proposition, and a retailer co-op advertising fund. A field sales team provides hands-on staff training at the 300 highest-volume accounts. This approach leverages Ardent's strongest asset but limits initial market reach and may produce slower ramp-up than the growth target demands.

optionB.name: Direct-to-Consumer E-Commerce Priority Launch
optionB.description: Ardent launches Verdant primarily through a branded e-commerce storefront and a national online marketplace, using targeted digital advertising and an influencer seeding program to build brand credibility before brick-and-mortar rollout. Gross margins are higher online, and customer data can inform retail placement decisions in year two. However, this approach bypasses Ardent's existing retailer relationships during the critical launch window and requires building e-commerce fulfillment capabilities the company does not currently possess at scale.

prompts.title: Stillwater Regional Medical Center: Service Expansion Decision
prompts.scenario: The board of Stillwater Regional Medical Center, a 340-bed nonprofit hospital serving a rural four-county area in eastern Oregon, must decide how to expand its capacity to address two pressing service gaps identified in its most recent community health needs assessment. The hospital has secured a one-time $14 million capital grant from a state rural health fund, and the grant terms require a commitment letter specifying the use of funds within 90 days. The board has determined that the full grant must be applied to one of two projects.
considerations: Stillwater's service area has the highest rate of unmet behavioral health need in the state, with the nearest inpatient psychiatric facility located 110 miles away.
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in all four counties, and residents currently must travel 75 miles for cardiac catheterization procedures.
Both projects must generate sufficient clinical revenue within four years to cover ongoing operating costs, as no recurring grant funding is available.
Stillwater's ability to recruit and retain specialist physicians is constrained by its rural location; any expansion that requires scarce specialty staff carries recruitment risk.

optionA.name: Establish an Inpatient Behavioral Health Unit
optionA.description: The hospital constructs and equips a 24-bed inpatient psychiatric unit, staffed by contracted psychiatric hospitalists and a newly recruited social work team. The unit addresses the most acute regional gap and aligns with state reimbursement incentives favoring behavioral health expansion. However, psychiatric reimbursement rates are lower than those for procedural specialties, creating uncertainty about achieving operating self-sufficiency within four years, and psychiatrist recruitment in rural Oregon has historically proven difficult.

optionB.name: Open a Cardiac Catheterization Laboratory
optionB.description: The hospital builds and equips a single-suite cardiac catheterization lab, allowing interventional cardiology procedures that currently require patient transfer. Procedural cardiology carries strong reimbursement and high demand in an aging, high-risk population, supporting a clearer path to financial self-sufficiency. The lab requires recruiting at least one interventional cardiologist, a position that typically commands a compensation package straining the hospital's existing physician employment budget and may take 18 months or more to fill.

prompts.title: Blue Ridge Farm Cooperative: Equipment-Sharing Program Redesign
prompts.scenario: The steering committee of the Blue Ridge Farm Cooperative, a 67-member agricultural cooperative in the Virginia Piedmont, must redesign its shared-equipment program after a member survey revealed widespread dissatisfaction with scheduling conflicts and maintenance delays. The cooperative's equipment fleet — valued at $1.9 million — includes tractors, planters, and harvest machinery used across diverse crop calendars. The committee must present a revised program structure at the annual member meeting in six weeks. Two redesign proposals have been developed.
considerations: Scheduling equity is the members' top-rated concern; smaller operations have repeatedly lost access to equipment during critical planting and harvest windows to larger member farms.
Equipment maintenance costs have risen 22 percent over three years; the cooperative's reserve fund covers only 60 percent of projected replacement needs over the next decade.
Member farms range from 40 to 800 acres and grow different crops; any scheduling system must accommodate significant variation in timing and equipment type.
The cooperative's bylaws require that any new fee or dues structure be approved by a two-thirds member vote, making financial redesign politically sensitive.

optionA.name: Tiered Reservation System with Priority Credits
optionA.description: The cooperative implements a digital reservation platform in which each member farm receives an equal annual allocation of priority credits used to secure first-access windows during peak periods; credits not used in a season expire and cannot accumulate. A modest per-use fee replaces the flat annual assessment, with revenue directed to the maintenance reserve. Smaller farms gain structural protection during critical windows, but the per-use fee structure requires member approval and may face resistance from high-volume users whose effective costs would rise substantially.

optionB.name: Subfleet Specialization with Designated User Groups
optionB.description: The cooperative divides the fleet into three specialized subfleets — grain, livestock-support, and specialty-crop — and assigns each member to a subfleet based on primary enterprise type. Each subfleet schedules its own equipment independently, reducing cross-enterprise conflicts and simplifying maintenance tracking by use type. This model requires no new fee structure and can be adopted by committee resolution, but it reduces overall fleet flexibility, may strand equipment in one subfleet during slow periods while another faces shortages, and could disadvantage diversified farms that operate across more than one enterprise type.
